learn.hook: Fold a sheet of paper in half again and again. After just 10 folds it would have 1024 layers! Doubling grows faster than you think.
points: In 2⁵, 2 is the base and 5 is the exponent (power). 2⁵ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32.
Each paper fold doubles the layers: after n folds there are 2ⁿ layers.
Powers grow very fast: 2¹⁰ = 1024 is much bigger than 10² = 100, even though both use a 2 and a 10.
A negative base with an even exponent gives a positive answer: (−2)⁴ = 16. With an odd exponent it stays negative: (−2)³ = −8.
(−1) to an even power is 1; (−1) to an odd power is −1.

example.q: Write 1,00,000 as a power of 10 and 81 as a power of 3.

learn.reallife: Messages forwarded on phones, a chain of Diwali greetings where each person sends to 2 more, and computer memory sizes (1024 MB) all grow in powers.

quiz.q: Aisha folds a sheet of paper in half 6 times. How many layers does it have now?
quiz.explain: Each fold doubles the layers, so 6 folds give 2⁶ = 64 layers.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 2 × 6 instead of 2 to the power 6

quiz.q: What is the value of (−2)⁴?
quiz.explain: (−2) × (−2) × (−2) × (−2) = 4 × 4 = 16. Four negative signs pair up to make a positive answer.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the negative sign even though the exponent is even

quiz.q: Which is greater, 2¹⁰ or 10²?
quiz.explain: 2¹⁰ = 1024 and 10² = 100. Swapping base and exponent changes the value a lot.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a bigger base always means a bigger value

quiz.q: Riya writes 81 as a power of 3. What is the exponent?
quiz.explain: 81 = 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 3⁴, so the exponent is 4.
quiz.mistake: Divides 81 by 3 instead of counting how many 3s multiply to 81

quiz.q: What is (−1)¹⁰¹?
quiz.explain: 101 is odd, so one −1 is left without a partner. (−1) to an odd power is −1.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the base by the exponent

quiz.q: A farmer puts 1 grain on day 1 and doubles the grains every day. How many grains does he put on day 11?
quiz.explain: Day 1 has 2⁰ = 1 grain, day 2 has 2¹, so day 11 has 2¹⁰ = 1024 grains.
quiz.mistake: Uses 2¹¹ and forgets that day 1 starts at 1 grain

quiz.q: How can 64 be written as a power of 4?
quiz.mistake: Divides 64 by 4 to get 16 and uses that as the exponent

quiz.q: In the Indian system, what is 10⁶ called?
quiz.explain: 10⁶ = 10,00,000, which is ten lakh (one million). 1 lakh is 10⁵ and 1 crore is 10⁷.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the place names lakh and crore

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: What does 2⁵ mean? Isn't it just 2 × 5 = 10?
teach.praise: Oh! It is 2 multiplied by itself 5 times: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32, not 10. Thank you!
teach.nudge: How many times is 2 written down when we work out 2⁵? And what is the answer?

revise.summary: In 2⁵, 2 is the base and 5 is the exponent, so 2⁵ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32. Powers grow very fast, and a negative base gives a positive answer for an even exponent and a negative one for an odd exponent.
focus: Identify the base and exponent and evaluate powers
Write numbers like 1,00,000 or 81 as powers
Compare powers such as 2¹⁰ and 10²
Find the sign of powers of negative numbers, including (−1)ⁿ
traps: Don't multiply base × exponent: 2⁶ = 64, not 12
A bigger base does not always mean a bigger value: 2¹⁰ > 10²
Don't keep a minus sign with an even exponent

topics.title: Folding paper: the power of doubling

learn.hook: Fold a thin sheet of paper in half 46 times (if you could!) and the pile would stretch past the Moon. Doubling is that powerful.
points: Every fold doubles the thickness. If the sheet starts t thick, after n folds it is t × 2ⁿ thick.
10 folds multiply the thickness by 2¹⁰ = 1024. A sheet 0.001 cm thick becomes about 1 cm thick.

After 30 folds the same sheet would be 0.001 × 2³⁰ cm ≈ 10.7 km tall — far taller than the Burj Khalifa (about 828 m) and even Mount Everest. After 46 folds it would be about 7 lakh km, more than the Earth–Moon distance (about 3,84,000 km).
Adding the same amount each time is linear growth: 2, 4, 6, 8, ... Multiplying by the same amount is exponential growth: 2, 4, 8, 16, ... Exponential growth soon leaves linear growth far behind.
A ladder to the Moon with 1 m steps would need 38,40,00,000 steps, but doubling gets there in fewer than 50 folds.

example.q: A card 0.01 cm thick is folded 5 times. How thick is the pile?
steps: Each fold doubles: 5 folds multiply by 2⁵ = 32

learn.reallife: Viral videos spread like folding paper: if each viewer shares with 2 friends, the views double again and again.

quiz.q: A sheet 0.1 mm thick is folded in half 4 times. How thick is the pile?
quiz.explain: 4 folds multiply the thickness by 2⁴ = 16, and 0.1 × 16 = 1.6 mm.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by the number of folds instead of by 2 each time

quiz.q: By how much do 10 folds multiply the thickness of a sheet?
quiz.explain: Each fold doubles, so 10 folds multiply by 2¹⁰ = 1024.
quiz.mistake: Adds 2 for each fold, or stops at 9 doublings

quiz.q: After how many folds is a sheet 128 times as thick as before?
quiz.explain: 128 = 2⁷, so it takes 7 folds.
quiz.mistake: Halves 128 instead of finding the power of 2

quiz.q: Mohan starts with ₹1 and doubles it every day. Sita starts with ₹1 and adds ₹100 every day. After 10 days, who has more?
quiz.explain: Mohan has 1 × 2¹⁰ = ₹1024. Sita has 1 + 10 × 100 = ₹1001. Doubling overtakes adding.
quiz.mistake: Treats doubling as adding 2 each day

quiz.q: A sheet 0.001 cm thick is folded 20 times. About how thick is the pile? (2²⁰ ≈ 10,48,576)
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by 20 instead of by 2²⁰

quiz.q: The Moon is about 3,84,000 km away. Would a 0.001 cm sheet folded 46 times reach it?
options: Yes — the pile would be about 7 lakh km
No — it would be about 46 cm
No — it would be about 1 km
quiz.explain: 2⁴⁶ ≈ 7 × 10¹³, so the pile is about 7 × 10¹⁰ cm = 7 × 10⁵ km, more than 3,84,000 km.
steps: Answer: Yes — the pile would be about 7 lakh km
quiz.mistake: Thinks 46 small doublings can only give a small height

quiz.q: Which kind of growth is shown by 3, 6, 9, 12, 15?
quiz.explain: The gap is always 3, so the same amount is added each time. That is linear growth.
steps: Answer: Linear — 3 is added each time
quiz.mistake: Mixes up adding a fixed amount with multiplying

quiz.q: A ladder adds 25 cm of height for each step. How many steps are needed to climb 1 km?
quiz.explain: 1 km = 1000 m and each step is 0.25 m, so 1000 ÷ 0.25 = 4000 steps. Linear growth is slow!
quiz.mistake: Forgets to change km into metres

teach.ask: Gappu thinks folding paper 30 times only makes it 30 times thicker. Explain what really happens!
teach.praise: Oh! Every fold doubles, so 30 folds multiply by 2³⁰ — over 100 crore! My nest could reach the sky!
teach.nudge: Does each fold add the same amount, or multiply? What does that do after many folds?

revise.summary: Every fold doubles the thickness, so a sheet t thick is t × 2ⁿ thick after n folds. This doubling is exponential growth, which soon leaves adding the same amount (linear growth) far behind.
focus: Find the thickness after n folds using t × 2ⁿ
Find how many folds give a certain multiple
Tell linear growth from exponential growth
Compare huge doubling results with real distances
remember: Linear: add the same amount (2, 4, 6, 8); exponential: multiply by the same amount (2, 4, 8, 16)
About 46 folds of a 0.001 cm sheet would pass the Moon (≈ 3,84,000 km)
traps: Don't multiply by the number of folds: 4 folds multiply by 2⁴ = 16, not 4
Don't treat doubling as adding 2 each time
Don't compare lengths in different units (1 km = 1000 m)

learn.hook: Can you work out 2²⁰ ÷ 2¹⁸ in one second? With the laws of exponents, you can: it is just 2² = 4!
points: Same base, multiply → add the exponents: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ. So 3² × 3⁴ = 3⁶.
Same base, divide → subtract the exponents: aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ. So 7⁹ ÷ 7⁴ = 7⁵.
Power of a power → multiply the exponents: (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ. So (5²)³ = 5⁶.
Same exponent: aᵐ × bᵐ = (ab)ᵐ. So 2³ × 5³ = 10³ = 1000.
Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1, and a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ. So 9⁰ = 1 and 2⁻³ = 1/8.
learn.reallife: Scientists and computer engineers use these laws every day, for example to say that 2¹⁰ × 2¹⁰ bytes is 2²⁰ bytes (about one million).

games.title: Law or flaw?
items: Keep the base and add the exponents: 3² × 3³ = 3⁵ = 243.
a⁰ = 1 for every non-zero number a
aⁿ ÷ aⁿ = aⁿ⁻ⁿ = a⁰, and any non-zero number divided by itself is 1.
Power of a power: multiply the exponents, 3 × 2 = 6.
A negative exponent means the reciprocal: 5⁻¹ = 1/5¹.

quiz.q: Simplify 3⁴ × 3².
quiz.explain: Same base, multiplying: add the exponents. 4 + 2 = 6, so the answer is 3⁶.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the exponents or multiplies the bases

quiz.q: What is the value of (2⁵ × 2³) ÷ 2⁶?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts before adding, or stops at 2⁸ = 256

quiz.q: When (4²)³ is written as a single power of 4, what is the exponent?
quiz.explain: Power of a power: multiply the exponents. 2 × 3 = 6, so (4²)³ = 4⁶.
quiz.mistake: Adds the exponents (2 + 3 = 5) instead of multiplying

quiz.q: What is 2025⁰?
quiz.explain: Any non-zero number raised to the power 0 equals 1.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a power of 0 makes the number 0

quiz.q: What is 5⁻²?
quiz.explain: A negative exponent means the reciprocal: 5⁻² = 1/5² = 1/25.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a negative exponent makes the answer negative

quiz.q: What is 2³ × 5³?
quiz.explain: Same exponent: 2³ × 5³ = (2 × 5)³ = 10³ = 1000. Check: 8 × 125 = 1000.
quiz.mistake: Adds the exponents to get 10⁶ or multiplies 2 × 5 × 3

quiz.q: Kabir says 2³ × 3² = 6⁵. What is the correct value of 2³ × 3²?
quiz.explain: The bases are different and so are the exponents, so no law joins them. Just calculate: 8 × 9 = 72.
quiz.mistake: Adds exponents even though the bases are different

quiz.q: Which of these is equal to 1/8?
quiz.mistake: Thinks a negative exponent gives a negative number

teach.ask: Gappu scratches his feathers: How do I quickly simplify 3⁴ × 3²? Do I multiply the 4 and the 2?
teach.praise: Keep the same base and add the powers: 3⁴ × 3² = 3⁶. Now I can do it fast!
teach.nudge: When the bases are the same and we multiply, what do we do with the exponents — add or multiply?

revise.summary: With the same base, multiplying adds exponents and dividing subtracts them; a power of a power multiplies them. With the same exponent, aᵐ × bᵐ = (ab)ᵐ. Also a⁰ = 1 and a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.
focus: Simplify products and quotients of powers with the same base
Use the power-of-a-power law
Use aᵐ × bᵐ = (ab)ᵐ
Evaluate zero and negative exponents
traps: Don't add exponents when the bases are different: 2³ × 3² ≠ 6⁵
Don't add exponents for a power of a power: (4²)³ = 4⁶
A negative exponent does not make the answer negative: 5⁻² = 1/25

learn.hook: What is the last digit of 2¹⁰⁰? Nobody multiplies it out — a repeating pattern tells you in seconds.
points: Prime factorisations look neat with exponents: 32400 = 2⁴ × 3⁴ × 5², and 720 = 2⁴ × 3² × 5.
Same exponent, dividing: mᵃ ÷ nᵃ = (m ÷ n)ᵃ. So 15³ ÷ 5³ = 3³ = 27.
Change bases to match: 4 = 2², 8 = 2³, 9 = 3², 27 = 3³. So 8⁴ ÷ 4⁵ = 2¹² ÷ 2¹⁰ = 2² = 4.

Units digits of powers repeat: powers of 2 end in 2, 4, 8, 6, 2, 4, ... (a cycle of 4). So 2¹⁰⁰ ends in 6, since 100 is a multiple of 4. Powers of 3 end in 3, 9, 7, 1; powers of 4 in 4, 6; powers of 9 in 9, 1.
learn.reallife: Computer scientists rewrite numbers as powers of 2 all the time — memory sizes like 1024 MB = 2¹⁰ MB.

quiz.q: How is 32400 written in exponential form?
quiz.mistake: Miscounts one of the prime factors

quiz.q: What is 15³ ÷ 5³?
quiz.explain: Same exponent: 15³ ÷ 5³ = (15 ÷ 5)³ = 3³ = 27.
quiz.mistake: Divides the bases but forgets to keep the exponent

quiz.q: Simplify 8⁴ ÷ 4⁵.
quiz.explain: Write both as powers of 2: 2¹² ÷ 2¹⁰ = 2² = 4.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the exponents without first making the bases the same

quiz.q: What is 27² ÷ 9³?
quiz.explain: 27² = (3³)² = 3⁶ and 9³ = (3²)³ = 3⁶. So the answer is 3⁶ ÷ 3⁶ = 1.
quiz.mistake: Divides the bases 27 ÷ 9 and keeps an exponent

quiz.q: What is the units digit of 2²⁰²⁵?
quiz.explain: Powers of 2 end in 2, 4, 8, 6 and repeat every 4. 2025 = 4 × 506 + 1, so 2²⁰²⁵ ends like 2¹, in 2.
quiz.mistake: Assumes an odd exponent always gives 8

quiz.q: What is the units digit of 3¹⁰⁰?
quiz.explain: Powers of 3 end in 3, 9, 7, 1 and repeat every 4. 100 is a multiple of 4, so 3¹⁰⁰ ends like 3⁴ = 81, in 1.
quiz.mistake: Uses the cycle of 2 instead of the cycle of 3

quiz.q: What is 12⁴ ÷ 4⁴?
quiz.mistake: Divides the bases and drops the power

quiz.q: Which of these equals 6⁵?
quiz.mistake: Splits the base but puts the power on only one factor, or adds

teach.ask: Gappu must find the last digit of 3⁵⁰ without multiplying 50 times. Help!
teach.praise: Clever! The last digits go 3, 9, 7, 1 and repeat. 50 leaves remainder 2, so it ends in 9!
teach.nudge: Do the last digits of powers of 3 follow a pattern? How long is it?

revise.summary: Exponents make prime factorisations neat, like 720 = 2⁴ × 3² × 5. To divide powers, use mᵃ ÷ nᵃ = (m ÷ n)ᵃ or first rewrite bases to match, and use repeating cycles to find units digits of big powers.
focus: Write numbers in exponential form using prime factors
Divide powers with the same exponent
Change bases (4 = 2², 9 = 3²) before dividing
Find the units digit of a large power using its cycle
remember: Units digits of powers of 2 cycle 2, 4, 8, 6; of 3 cycle 3, 9, 7, 1
traps: Don't subtract exponents until the bases are the same
Don't drop the exponent after dividing the bases: 12⁴ ÷ 4⁴ = 3⁴ = 81
Use the right cycle length: powers of 3 repeat every 4, not every 2

topics.title: Powers in stories: tripling, doubling and counting choices

learn.hook: How many number plates can India make with just 2 letters and 4 digits? Over 67 lakh — and powers tell you why.
points: Repeated tripling: if shining stones triple every day starting from 1, there are 1, 3, 9, 27, ... — 3ⁿ stones after n days.

Magical pond: if lotuses double every day and cover the pond on day 30, they covered half of it on day 29. If fish double for 5 days and then triple for 3 days, their number is multiplied by 2⁵ × 3³ = 864.
Multiplication principle: 3 shirts and 4 pants make 3 × 4 = 12 outfits. A 3-digit lock using 0–9 has 10 × 10 × 10 = 10³ = 1000 codes.
Number plates with 2 letters then 4 digits: 26² × 10⁴ = 67,60,000 plates.
To give unique codes to many items, find the smallest power that is big enough: 5000 students need 4-digit codes, since 10³ = 1000 is too few but 10⁴ = 10000 is enough.

example.q: How many 4-digit PINs can be made from the digits 0–9?
steps: Each of the 4 places has 10 choices

learn.reallife: Every UPI PIN, phone number and vehicle number in India is designed using this multiplication principle.

quiz.q: A cave has 1 shining stone. Every day the number of shining stones triples. How many shine after 5 days?
quiz.explain: Tripling 5 times gives 3⁵ = 243.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 3 by 5 or uses 5³

quiz.q: Lotuses double every day and fully cover a pond on day 30. On which day was half the pond covered?
quiz.explain: Doubling the half-cover gives the full cover, so half was covered one day earlier, on day 29.
quiz.mistake: Halves the number of days instead of going back one doubling

quiz.q: A pond has 10 fish. Their number doubles every week. How many fish are there after 3 weeks?
quiz.mistake: Adds 10 each week or doubles one time too many

quiz.q: Insects double for 4 days and then triple for 2 days. By what number is their population multiplied?
quiz.explain: Doubling 4 times multiplies by 2⁴ = 16; tripling twice multiplies by 3² = 9. Together 16 × 9 = 144.
quiz.mistake: Adds the effects instead of multiplying them

quiz.q: Ananya has 4 kurtas, 3 pyjamas and 2 dupattas. How many different outfits of one of each can she make?
quiz.explain: Multiply the choices: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24.
quiz.mistake: Adds the choices instead of multiplying

quiz.q: How many 4-digit PINs can be made with the digits 0–9 (digits may repeat)?
quiz.explain: Each of the 4 places has 10 choices: 10⁴ = 10000.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 4 by 10, or forgets that 0000 is also a PIN

quiz.q: A number plate has 2 letters (A–Z) followed by 3 digits (0–9). How many plates are possible?
quiz.mistake: Uses 26 × 2 instead of 26² for the letters

quiz.q: A library wants a different code for each of its 700 books, using only letters A–Z. What is the smallest number of letters each code needs?
quiz.explain: 1 letter gives 26 codes and 2 letters give 26² = 676 — not enough. 3 letters give 26³ = 17576, enough.
quiz.mistake: Stops at 2 letters without checking that 676 < 700

teach.ask: Gappu has 3 hats and 5 bow ties. He thinks he has 8 looks. Is he right?
teach.praise: 15 looks! Every hat goes with every bow tie, so we multiply. Fashion bird!
teach.nudge: Do you add or multiply the number of choices?

revise.summary: Repeated doubling or tripling gives powers: tripling from 1 gives 3ⁿ after n days. The multiplication principle counts choices by multiplying, so a 3-digit lock has 10³ = 1000 codes.
focus: Solve repeated doubling and tripling stories
Work backwards in doubling stories (half covered one day earlier)
Count outfits, PINs and number plates by multiplying choices
Find the smallest code length that gives enough codes
remember: Tripling from 1 for n days gives 3ⁿ
If something doubles daily and is full on day 30, it was half full on day 29
Multiplication principle: choices multiply (3 shirts × 4 pants = 12)
n places with 10 digits each give 10ⁿ codes
traps: Don't add choices: multiply them
Don't halve the number of days in a doubling story
Don't choose a code length that is too short: 26² = 676 is less than 700

topics.title: Zero and negative exponents, and power lines

learn.hook: Cut a 1 m ribbon in half, then half again, and again... The pieces are 2⁻¹, 2⁻², 2⁻³ metres long. Yes — negative powers are real!
points: Going down the powers of 2 divides by 2 each step: 2³ = 8, 2² = 4, 2¹ = 2, 2⁰ = 1, 2⁻¹ = 1/2, 2⁻² = 1/4. Halving a 1 m strip again and again gives these lengths.
So n⁰ = 1 for any n that is not 0, and n⁻ᵃ = 1/nᵃ. 0⁰ is not given a value this way, because getting it from 0ᵃ ÷ 0ᵃ would mean dividing by 0.
Power line: mark 4⁻², 4⁻¹, 4⁰, 4¹, 4², 4³ at equal steps. Multiplying by 4² means moving 2 steps right; dividing by 4³ means moving 3 steps left.
All the laws work for every integer exponent: 5⁻³ × 5⁵ = 5², (2⁻²)³ = 2⁻⁶, and 3⁴ ÷ 3⁷ = 3⁻³ = 1/27.
learn.reallife: Scientists write tiny sizes with negative powers: a hair is about 10⁻⁴ m thick.

quiz.q: What is 2⁻⁵?
quiz.explain: 2⁻⁵ = 1/2⁵ = 1/32. A negative exponent means the reciprocal, not a negative number.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a negative exponent makes the answer negative

quiz.q: A 1 m strip is cut in half 4 times, keeping one piece each time. How long is the last piece?
quiz.explain: Each cut halves the length: 1 × 2⁻⁴ = 1/16 m.
quiz.mistake: Stops one halving early

quiz.q: What is 10⁻³?
quiz.mistake: Treats the negative exponent as a minus sign

quiz.q: Simplify 5⁻³ × 5⁵.
quiz.explain: Add the exponents: −3 + 5 = 2, so 5² = 25.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the exponents or multiplies them

quiz.q: What is 3⁴ ÷ 3⁷?
quiz.explain: Subtract the exponents: 4 − 7 = −3, and 3⁻³ = 1/27.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the smaller exponent from the larger and loses the reciprocal

quiz.q: On a power line of 4, start at 4², multiply by 4³, then divide by 4⁶. Where do you end?
quiz.explain: Move 3 steps right, then 6 steps left: 2 + 3 − 6 = −1. 4⁻¹ = 1/4.
quiz.mistake: Moves the wrong way for division

quiz.q: Why is 0⁰ not given the value 1 by the rule n⁰ = nᵃ ÷ nᵃ?
options: Because the rule only works for n = 1
quiz.explain: n⁰ = nᵃ ÷ nᵃ = 1 works because we divide a number by itself. For n = 0 this would be 0 ÷ 0, which is not defined.
steps: Answer: Because 0ᵃ ÷ 0ᵃ would mean dividing by 0
quiz.mistake: Thinks the zero-exponent rule works the same for a zero base

quiz.q: Simplify (2⁻²)³ × 2⁸.
quiz.mistake: Adds the exponents in the power-of-a-power step

teach.ask: Gappu thinks 2⁻³ is −8. Can you explain what a negative exponent really means?
teach.praise: Ah! 2⁻³ means 1 ÷ 2³ = 1/8 — a small piece, not a negative number!
teach.nudge: What happens each time you go one step down the powers of 2?

revise.summary: Going down the powers of 2 divides by 2 each step, giving 2⁰ = 1 and 2⁻¹ = 1/2. So n⁰ = 1 and n⁻ᵃ = 1/nᵃ, and all the exponent laws work for every integer exponent.
focus: Evaluate zero and negative powers
Use halving to explain negative exponents
Move along a power line for multiplying and dividing
Simplify expressions with negative exponents using the laws
remember: On a power line, multiplying by 4² moves 2 steps right; dividing by 4³ moves 3 steps left
0⁰ is not given a value this way, because 0ᵃ ÷ 0ᵃ means dividing by 0
traps: A negative exponent does not make the number negative: 2⁻⁵ = 1/32
Don't add exponents in a power of a power; multiply them: (2⁻²)³ = 2⁻⁶

topics.title: Powers of 10: expanded form and big-number names

learn.hook: 1 arab = 1 billion = 100 crore. Same number, three names! Powers of 10 help us switch between them.
points: Expanded form with powers of 10: 4705 = 4 × 10³ + 7 × 10² + 0 × 10¹ + 5 × 10⁰.
Decimal places use negative powers: 23.56 = 2 × 10¹ + 3 × 10⁰ + 5 × 10⁻¹ + 6 × 10⁻².
Indian names: lakh = 10⁵, crore = 10⁷, arab = 10⁹, kharab = 10¹¹. International names: thousand = 10³, million = 10⁶, billion = 10⁹.
So 1 million = 10 lakh, 1 crore = 10 million, and 1 billion = 1 arab = 100 crore.
A googol is 10¹⁰⁰ — 1 followed by 100 zeros. A googolplex is 10 to the power googol: 1 followed by a googol zeros, far too many ever to write down.

example.q: Write 50,306.07 in expanded form with powers of 10.

learn.reallife: News reports switch between '₹1 lakh crore' and '₹1 trillion' — both are 10¹² rupees.

quiz.explain: 30000 + 500 + 8 = 30508. The missing powers (10³ and 10¹) give zeros.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the place holders for the missing powers

quiz.q: In 2.045, the digit 4 stands for 4 × 10 to which power?
quiz.explain: 4 is in the hundredths place: 4/100 = 4 × 10⁻².
quiz.mistake: Counts the decimal places wrongly

quiz.q: 1 billion is how many crore?
quiz.explain: 1 billion = 10⁹ and 1 crore = 10⁷, so 10⁹ ÷ 10⁷ = 10² = 100.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up million and billion

quiz.q: 5 million is how many lakh?
quiz.explain: 5 million = 5 × 10⁶ = 50 × 10⁵, which is 50 lakh.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a million and a lakh are the same

quiz.q: How many zeros come after the 1 in a googol?
quiz.explain: A googol is 10¹⁰⁰, so 1 is followed by 100 zeros.
steps: So a googol has 100 zeros after the 1.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a googol with a googolplex or with 10¹⁰

quiz.q: Which power of 10 is 1 kharab?
quiz.explain: lakh 10⁵, crore 10⁷, arab 10⁹, kharab 10¹¹ — each Indian name is 100 times the one before.
quiz.mistake: Thinks each name is 10 times the previous

quiz.q: India's population is about 140 crore. How much is that in billions?
quiz.explain: 140 crore = 140 × 10⁷ = 1.4 × 10⁹, which is 1.4 billion.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 1 crore = 1 billion

quiz.q: Which is the expanded form of 0.305?
quiz.explain: 3 is in the tenths place (10⁻¹) and 5 is in the thousandths place (10⁻³).
quiz.mistake: Skips the zero in the hundredths place

teach.ask: Gappu's uncle says a film earned '1 arab'. Gappu has never heard of arab! How big is it?
teach.praise: 1 arab = 10⁹ = 1 billion = 100 crore. What a lot of popcorn money!
teach.nudge: Which power of 10 is an arab? How does it compare with a crore?

revise.summary: Any number can be written in expanded form with powers of 10, using negative powers for decimal places. Indian names (lakh 10⁵, crore 10⁷) and international names (million 10⁶, billion 10⁹) are all powers of 10.
focus: Write numbers and decimals in expanded form with powers of 10
Convert between lakh, crore, million and billion
Know the powers for arab and kharab
Know what a googol and a googolplex are
remember: 1 million = 10 lakh; 1 crore = 10 million; 1 billion = 100 crore
traps: Don't skip the zero places: 0.305 has 0 hundredths
A million is 10 lakh, not 1 lakh
1 billion is 100 crore, not 1 crore

learn.hook: The Sun is about 15,00,00,000 km away. Counting those zeros is tiring! Scientists simply write 1.5 × 10⁸ km.
points: Scientific notation (standard form) writes a number as a × 10ⁿ, where a is at least 1 and less than 10.
For a big number, move the decimal point left and count the jumps: 4,50,000 = 4.5 × 10⁵.
For a tiny number, move the decimal point right; the exponent becomes negative: 0.0005 = 5 × 10⁻⁴.
To compare two numbers in standard form, compare the powers of 10 first: 2 × 10⁸ is bigger than 9 × 10⁷.
In the Indian system, 1 lakh = 10⁵ and 1 crore = 10⁷.

example.q: The Moon is about 3,84,000 km from the Earth. Write this in scientific notation.
steps: Put the decimal after the first digit: 3.84
Count how many places the point moved: 5

learn.reallife: India's population (about 1.4 × 10⁹), distances to stars and the size of a virus are all written in scientific notation.

quiz.q: How is 5,60,000 written in scientific notation?
quiz.explain: Move the decimal point 5 places left: 5,60,000 = 5.6 × 10⁵. The first part must be between 1 and 10.
quiz.mistake: Counts the number of zeros (4) instead of the jumps of the decimal point

quiz.q: How is 0.00034 written in scientific notation?
quiz.explain: Move the decimal point 4 places right to get 3.4, so the exponent is −4.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the negative sign or miscounts the jumps

quiz.q: What is 2.5 × 10³ in usual form?
quiz.explain: Multiplying by 10³ moves the decimal point 3 places right: 2.5 → 2500.
quiz.mistake: Adds three zeros after 25 to get 25000

quiz.q: 1 crore is 10 raised to what power?
quiz.explain: 1 crore = 1,00,00,000, which has 7 zeros, so it is 10⁷.
quiz.mistake: Confuses crore with 10 lakh (10⁶)

quiz.q: Which is larger: 3 × 10⁸ or 9 × 10⁷?
quiz.explain: 3 × 10⁸ = 30 crore and 9 × 10⁷ = 9 crore. Compare the powers of 10 first.
quiz.mistake: Compares only the front numbers (9 > 3)

quiz.q: Light travels about 3 × 10⁸ m in one second. About how far does it travel in 2 seconds?
quiz.explain: Double the distance: 2 × 3 × 10⁸ = 6 × 10⁸ m. The power of 10 does not change.
quiz.mistake: Doubles the exponent as well as the number

quiz.q: A tiny bacterium is about 0.000002 m long. What is this in scientific notation?
quiz.explain: Move the point 6 places right to get 2, so the length is 2 × 10⁻⁶ m.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the zeros after the decimal point (5)

quiz.explain: Multiply the numbers (2 × 4 = 8) and add the exponents of 10 (3 + 2 = 5): 8 × 10⁵.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the exponents instead of adding them

teach.ask: Gappu blinks: How do I write 4,50,000 in scientific notation? There are so many zeros!
teach.praise: Move the decimal point to get 4.5, count 5 jumps, so 4.5 × 10⁵. Neat and short!
teach.nudge: Where should the decimal point go, and how do you know which power of 10 to use?

revise.summary: Scientific notation writes a number as a × 10ⁿ, with a at least 1 and less than 10. Move the decimal point and count the jumps: left for big numbers, right for tiny numbers (negative exponent).
focus: Write big and tiny numbers in scientific notation
Change scientific notation back to usual form
Compare numbers in standard form
Multiply numbers in standard form
traps: Count the jumps of the decimal point, not the zeros
Don't forget the minus sign for numbers less than 1
When multiplying, add the exponents; doubling 3 × 10⁸ gives 6 × 10⁸, not 6 × 10¹⁶

topics.title: Estimating big numbers and big times

learn.hook: Have you lived for a billion seconds? Not yet — you would need to be about 32 years old!
points: To estimate: (1) make a guess, (2) choose simple assumptions (a model), (3) calculate, (4) check whether the answer makes sense.
Tulabhara-style problems: a person is balanced against coins, fruits or grain. A 60 kg person = 60,000 g. If each coin weighs about 5 g, that is 60,000 ÷ 5 = 12,000 coins.
Time in powers of 10: 1 day = 86,400 s (about 10⁵ s); 10⁶ s ≈ 11.6 days; 1 year ≈ 3.15 × 10⁷ s; 10⁹ s ≈ 31.7 years.
A 13-year-old has lived about 13 × 365 = 4745 days ≈ 1,13,880 hours ≈ 4.1 × 10⁸ seconds.
Big counts become easy to compare as powers of 10: India's population is about 1.4 × 10⁹; a 10-litre bucket holds about 2 × 10⁵ drops if one drop is 0.05 ml.

example.q: At a tulabhara, a 50 kg child is balanced with bananas of about 125 g each. About how many bananas are needed?

learn.reallife: Planners estimate how many buses a festival needs or how much water a city drinks using the same guess–model–compute–check idea.

quiz.q: How many seconds are there in one day?
quiz.explain: 24 hours × 60 minutes × 60 seconds = 86,400 seconds.
quiz.mistake: Stops at minutes or seconds in one hour

quiz.q: About how long is 10⁶ seconds (one million seconds)?
quiz.explain: 10⁶ ÷ 86,400 ≈ 11.6, so a million seconds is about 11.6 days.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a million seconds is close to a year

quiz.q: About how long is 10⁹ seconds (one billion seconds)?
quiz.explain: A year is about 3.15 × 10⁷ s. 10⁹ ÷ (3.15 × 10⁷) ≈ 31.7 years.
quiz.mistake: Divides by the seconds in a day instead of a year

quiz.q: At a tulabhara, Ravi (45 kg) is balanced with coconuts of about 500 g each. About how many coconuts are needed?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to change kg into g

quiz.q: A ₹10 note weighs about 1 g. What value of ₹10 notes would balance a 50 kg person?
quiz.mistake: Counts the notes but forgets each is worth ₹10

quiz.q: Ignoring leap years, about how many days has a 12-year-old lived?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by 100 days a year, or slips a zero

quiz.q: Which order shows good estimation steps?
quiz.explain: First guess, then build a simple model with assumptions, calculate with it, and finally check if the answer is sensible.
steps: Answer: Guess → make assumptions → calculate → check
quiz.mistake: Skips the assumptions or the checking step

quiz.q: A drop of water is about 0.05 ml. About how many drops are in a 10-litre bucket?
quiz.mistake: Forgets that 1 litre = 1000 ml

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know how many seconds old he is. How would you estimate it?
teach.praise: Days × 24 × 60 × 60! I'm about 10⁸ seconds old, tweet!
teach.nudge: How many seconds are there in one day? How do you go from years to days?

revise.summary: To estimate, guess, choose simple assumptions, calculate, then check that the answer makes sense. Powers of 10 make big numbers and long times easy to compare: a day is about 10⁵ s and 10⁹ s is about 31.7 years.
focus: Follow the estimation steps: guess, assume, calculate, check
Solve tulabhara-style balancing problems with unit changes
Convert big numbers of seconds into days and years
Estimate counts like drops in a bucket
remember: 10⁶ s ≈ 11.6 days; 1 year ≈ 3.15 × 10⁷ s; 10⁹ s ≈ 31.7 years
traps: Don't divide kg by g (or litres by ml); change to the same unit first
A million seconds is about 11.6 days, not close to a year
Don't skip the assumptions or the checking step

topics.title: A pinch of history: Indian names for huge numbers

learn.hook: Long before calculators, Indian texts had names for numbers with 50 zeros. Ancient India loved big numbers!
points: Ancient Indian texts gave names to very large powers of ten, far beyond what daily life needed.
In the Buddhist text Lalitavistara, young Siddhartha names number after number, each 100 times the one before, going far beyond a koti (crore) up to tallakshana = 10⁵³.

Jaina and Pali (Buddhist) works use enormous numbers to describe time and the universe. Mahaviracharya (9th century CE), in his book Ganita Sara Sangraha, listed 24 names for the powers of ten one after another, from eka (1) up to 10²³.
Modern Indian names continue the lakh–crore pattern, each 100 times the last: arab 10⁹, kharab 10¹¹, neel 10¹³, padma 10¹⁵, shankh 10¹⁷, maha shankh 10¹⁹.
learn.reallife: Words like padma and shankh still appear in Indian number charts and quiz shows.

quiz.q: How many zeros does 1 padma have?
quiz.explain: 1 padma = 10¹⁵, so it is 1 followed by 15 zeros.
steps: The list goes arab 10⁹, kharab 10¹¹, neel 10¹³, padma 10¹⁵.
quiz.mistake: Confuses padma with neel or shankh

quiz.q: 1 shankh is how many padma?
quiz.explain: shankh = 10¹⁷ and padma = 10¹⁵, so 10¹⁷ ÷ 10¹⁵ = 100.
quiz.mistake: Thinks each name is 10 times the previous

quiz.q: In the modern Indian list, which name comes right after kharab?
quiz.explain: The order is arab, kharab, neel, padma, shankh.
steps: Modern Indian names, each 100 times the last: arab, kharab, neel, padma, shankh.
quiz.mistake: Skips a step in the list

quiz.q: Which book did Mahaviracharya write?
quiz.explain: Mahaviracharya (9th century CE) wrote the Ganita Sara Sangraha, which lists 24 names for powers of ten, up to 10²³.
steps: Mahaviracharya lived in the 9th century CE.
His book, the Ganita Sara Sangraha, lists 24 names for powers of ten.
Lalitavistara is a Buddhist text, not his book.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the authors of famous maths books

quiz.q: In the Lalitavistara story, each new number name is how many times the previous one?
quiz.explain: The names in the story grow by a factor of 100 at each step, going up to 10⁵³.
steps: In the Lalitavistara, Siddhartha names number after number.
Each new name is 100 times the one before.
quiz.mistake: Assumes each step is 10 times, as in place value

quiz.q: How many zeros does 1 maha shankh have?
quiz.explain: maha shankh = 10¹⁹, which is 100 times a shankh (10¹⁷).
steps: shankh = 10¹⁷, and the next name is 100 times bigger.
quiz.mistake: Stops at shankh

quiz.q: Which old Indian traditions are known for using enormous numbers?
quiz.explain: Jaina and Pali Buddhist works describe time and the universe using huge numbers.
steps: The topic says Jaina and Pali (Buddhist) works use enormous numbers.
They describe time and the universe with them.
So the answer is Jaina and Buddhist (Pali) texts.
quiz.mistake: Thinks very large numbers are only a modern idea

quiz.q: 1 neel is how many crore?
quiz.explain: neel = 10¹³ and crore = 10⁷, so 10¹³ ÷ 10⁷ = 10⁶ = 10 lakh.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the exponents wrongly

teach.ask: Gappu heard the word 'shankh' used for a number. How big is it, and where do such names come from?
teach.praise: Wow! Shankh is 10¹⁷, and ancient texts went even beyond. India was a big-number champion!
teach.nudge: What power of 10 is shankh? Which old texts used such huge numbers?

revise.summary: Ancient Indian texts named huge powers of ten. The Lalitavistara goes up to tallakshana = 10⁵³, Mahaviracharya listed 24 names up to 10²³, and modern Indian names grow by 100 each step from lakh and crore.
focus: Know the modern list: arab, kharab, neel, padma, shankh, maha shankh
Convert between these names using powers of 10
Know Mahaviracharya and the Ganita Sara Sangraha
Know the Lalitavistara story and Jaina and Pali uses of huge numbers
remember: arab 10⁹, kharab 10¹¹, neel 10¹³, padma 10¹⁵, shankh 10¹⁷, maha shankh 10¹⁹
Each modern name is 100 times the one before
Mahaviracharya (9th century CE), Ganita Sara Sangraha: 24 names up to 10²³
Lalitavistara: each name 100 times the last, up to tallakshana = 10⁵³
traps: Don't think each name is 10 times the previous one: it is 100 times
Don't skip neel between kharab and padma
Huge numbers are not only a modern idea

topics.title: Power puzzles: compare, always or never

learn.hook: Which is bigger, 4³ or 3⁴? 2⁸ or 8²? Guess first — the answers surprise many grown-ups!
points: Compare by working them out: 4³ = 64 but 3⁴ = 81; 2⁸ = 256 but 8² = 64; and 2⁴ = 4² = 16 is a rare tie.
Always, sometimes or never? 'An odd number to any power is odd' is always true. 'aⁿ is bigger than a' is only sometimes true (false for a = 1). '2ⁿ ends in 0' is never true.
Numbers that are both perfect squares and perfect cubes are sixth powers: 1, 64 (= 8² = 4³), 729 (= 27² = 9³), 4096, ...
In a 'make the biggest number' game with digits and powers, a bigger exponent usually helps more than a bigger base: 3⁵ = 243 beats 5³ = 125, and 9⁹ is far bigger than 99.
learn.reallife: Comparing powers helps you see why a 6-digit password is far safer than a 4-digit one: 10⁶ vs 10⁴ choices.

games.title: Always, sometimes or never?
items: An odd number to any power is odd
A perfect square is also a perfect cube

games.title: Bigger or smaller?
items: 64 is both a square and a cube

quiz.q: Which is larger: 4³ or 3⁴?
quiz.explain: 4³ = 64 and 3⁴ = 81, so 3⁴ is larger.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the bigger base always gives the bigger power

quiz.q: What is 2⁸ − 8²?
quiz.explain: 2⁸ = 256 and 8² = 64, so the difference is 192.
quiz.mistake: Thinks swapping base and exponent gives the same value

quiz.q: After 64, which is the next number that is both a perfect square and a perfect cube?
quiz.explain: Such numbers are sixth powers: 2⁶ = 64, then 3⁶ = 729 = 27² = 9³.
quiz.mistake: Picks a number that is only a cube or only a square

quiz.q: How many numbers from 1 to 1000 are both perfect squares and perfect cubes?
quiz.explain: They are the sixth powers 1, 64 and 729. The next, 4096, is too big.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that 1 counts

quiz.q: 'For any whole number a and n > 1, aⁿ is bigger than a.' This is...
quiz.explain: It is true for 3² = 9 > 3, but false for 1² = 1 and 0² = 0.
quiz.mistake: Tests only one or two examples

quiz.q: Using the digits 3 and 5 once each in the form aᵇ, what is the largest number you can make?
quiz.explain: 3⁵ = 243 and 5³ = 125, so 3⁵ is larger.
quiz.mistake: Puts the bigger digit as the base

quiz.q: Which is the largest?
quiz.explain: 100² = 10⁴, 10¹⁰, and 100¹⁰ = 10²⁰, while 2¹⁰⁰ = (2¹⁰)¹⁰ > (10³)¹⁰ = 10³⁰. So 2¹⁰⁰ is largest.
quiz.mistake: Judges by the size of the base

quiz.q: What is 2⁵ − 5²?
quiz.explain: 2⁵ = 32 and 5² = 25, so the difference is 7.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 2⁵ and 5² are equal

teach.ask: Gappu bets that 5³ is bigger than 3⁵ because 5 is bigger. Will he win the bet?
teach.praise: Oops, I lose! 3⁵ = 243 beats 5³ = 125 — the exponent matters a lot.
teach.nudge: Did you work out both numbers? Which part of a power makes it grow fastest?

revise.summary: Compare powers by working them out: 3⁴ = 81 beats 4³ = 64, and 2⁴ = 4² is a rare tie. Test 'always, sometimes or never' claims with examples, and remember numbers that are both squares and cubes are sixth powers.
focus: Compare powers with swapped base and exponent
Decide if a statement about powers is always, sometimes or never true
Find numbers that are both perfect squares and perfect cubes
Make the largest number from given digits as a power
remember: Squares that are also cubes are sixth powers: 1, 64, 729, 4096
An odd number to any power is odd
A bigger exponent usually helps more than a bigger base: 3⁵ = 243 > 5³ = 125
traps: A bigger base does not always give a bigger power
Don't think swapping base and exponent keeps the value; it usually changes it
Don't forget 1 when counting numbers that are both squares and cubes
